## Series result

**Winner: me (Seat B), 2–0 in a best-of-3.**

| Game | Winner | Rounds | Final chips | Final dice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | B | 6 | B 111 – A 89 | B 4 – A 0 |
| 2 | B | 6 | B 112 – A 88 | B 4 – A 0 |

Both games ended by dice elimination — A was reduced from five dice to zero in six rounds each time, and never won a game.

## What decided it

Two exploitable regularities in A's play, both confirmed by reveals:

- **Its opening bid was an honest hand report.** A always opened at *(its best-face count + 1)* on its genuine longest suit, breaking ties toward the **lowest** face. That let me reconstruct its hand outright. In game 2 round 2 its "2 twos" implied no pair and no wild, so I called its "3 fours" as false — it held 5,2,4,6, exactly as deduced. In the last round of each game it was down to one die, and the opening face named that die precisely (a 6, then a 3).
- **It challenged whenever the standing bid looked under ~40% from its seat**, applying that test *before* considering a raise — in game 2 round 1 it challenged at 21% while holding an 86.8% raise. So the winning move was repeatedly to name the **highest bid my own dice already guaranteed** and let it challenge into a certain loss. Four of my round wins came that way, including bids that were true with probability 1 (3 twos, 4 fives, 2 sixes).

The strongest version was the closing bid of each game — a *closed trap* rather than merely a true bid: "4 threes" with two wilds was exactly true, so challenging failed, and every legal raise was arithmetically dead. A had no winning reply.

I lost three rounds across the series. Two were genuine variance on correct reads (game 1 round 3: A held 1,4,4 making its bid true by exactly one; game 2 round 3: I had pinned A to {1,2,3} or {2,2,3} and the likelier hand hit). The third, game 2 round 3, was a structural trap I walked into — every face was capped at the same total of 4, so whoever had to bid past that ceiling lost. I adjusted afterward by favouring hands with depth or a wild.

I declined the pot-raise declaration throughout: chips don't decide the series, and I wasn't willing to risk locked rounds on mechanics I hadn't tested.
